ancient.name: Sima de los Huesos
ancient.story_individual:
Around 400,000 years ago, a hominin died and their remains ended up in what would become known as Sima de los Huesos (Pit of Bones) in northern Spain. The individual's remains, including a femur which would later yield crucial DNA evidence, were preserved alongside approximately 28 other individuals in the cave system at Atapuerca. While researchers cannot determine this individual's biological sex, they know they belonged to a population that showed Neanderthal-like features in their skeletal morphology.

The remarkable preservation of their DNA was made possible by the stable, cold conditions within the cave. When the femur was analyzed in 2014, the DNA retrieved from it represented the oldest human DNA ever sequenced, pushing back the boundaries of ancient DNA research by hundreds of thousands of years. The mitochondrial DNA unexpectedly showed closer affinity to Denisovans than to Neanderthals, despite the skeletal characteristics of the population.

The recovery of such ancient DNA was a major technical achievement that required innovative methods to deal with highly degraded genetic material. While we don't know the details of this individual's life - what they ate, how they lived, or how they died - their genetic legacy has provided crucial insights into human evolution and the complex relationships between ancient hominin populations.

Subsequent nuclear DNA analysis of Sima de los Huesos hominins revealed a closer connection to Neanderthals than the mtDNA initially suggested, adding another fascinating layer to this individual's story.

References

  • Meyer, M., Fu, Q., Aximu-Petri, A. et al. A mitochondrial genome sequence of a hominin from Sima de los Huesos. Nature 505, 403–406 (2014). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12788

  • Meyer, M., Arsuaga, JL., de Filippo, C. et al. Nuclear DNA sequences from the Middle Pleistocene Sima de los Huesos hominins. Nature 531, 504–507 (2016). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature17405

Pictured: Cranium 17 of the Sima de los Huesos, from an individual from the same location and time period. Nohemi Sala, Juan Luis Arsuaga, Ana Pantoja-Pérez, Adrián Pablos, Ignacio Martínez, Rolf M. Quam, Asier Gómez-Olivencia, José María Bermúdez de Castro, Eudald Carbonell, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

famous.name: GMUNK
famous.story_individual:
Bradley G. Munkowitz, professionally known as GMUNK, is a renowned digital artist, live-action director, and motion designer based in Berkeley, California. Born and raised in Minneapolis, he had a unique upbringing influenced by his free-spirited mother, who lived with the Lakota Sioux tribe in South Dakota for three years to find herself, fostering deep conversations on purpose, fulfillment, and the supernatural.

Munkowitz initially studied at Humboldt State University and entered the industry through Flash animation, which he describes as an early form of motion graphics. His career began as an interactive designer at Vir2L Studios in London, where he created award-winning web experiences on his site GMUNK.com, inspiring interactive storytelling. Over two decades, GMUNK has worked with top studios like BUCK, Prologue Films, Transistorstudios, and Bot & Dolly, collaborating on global brands such as Nike, Maserati, and Audi. Notable highlights include designing holographic interfaces for films like TRON: Legacy (2010) and Oblivion (2013), robotic projection mapping for BOX (2013), and global branding, including the iconic "Hero" desktop wallpaper for Windows 10 (2015).

GMUNK's signature style blends psychedelic themes, sci-fi influences, and richly textured palettes, spanning motion design, experiential art, photography, robotics, and NFTs. Recent projects include concert visuals for Billie Eilish's 2024 World Tour, the Rivian Borealis experiential activation at Art Basel (2025), digital art collections like InfraMunk vol1 (2021), and illuminated sculptures such as The Totem (2022). He remains active in the global design community, delivering lectures worldwide and continuously reinventing his craft through new mediums and collaborations.

Pictured: GMUNK at Burning Man

famous.name: Roger Sherman Loomis
famous.story_individual:
Roger Sherman Loomis was one of the most prominent Arthurian scholars of the 20th century. Throughout his career he was a professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Columbia University, and the University of Oxford. He attended the first International Arthurian Congress and later was president of the American branch of the International Arthurian Society.

Loomis’ work studied connections between Arthurian legends and Celtic mythology, focusing on the legends surrounding the Holy Grail. He surmised that the stories of the Holy Grail were highly influenced by Welsh and Irish myths about magic cauldrons, especially the tale of Brân Fendigaidd, or Bran the Blessed, and his life-restoring cauldron.

Loomis was the author of numerous books and won the Haskins Medal of the Medieval Academy of America for his book Arthurian Tradition and Chretien de Troyes.

Roger Sherman Loomis’s mtDNA haplogroup has been inferred from mtFull testing of matrilineal relatives as shared on WikiTree.

Biographical information sourced from Wikipedia. Pictured: Roger Sherman Loomis, 1930 Arthurian Society in Truro, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

famous.name: Bono (Paul David Hewson)
famous.story_individual:
Paul David Hewson, better known as Bono, is one of the most influential figures in both modern music and global activism. As the lead singer and primary lyricist of the Irish rock band U2, which he co-founded in Dublin in 1976, Bono has helped shape the landscape of contemporary rock music while using his platform to advocate for social justice causes worldwide.

His musical achievements with U2 are remarkable, including 22 Grammy Awards and induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. However, Bono's impact extends far beyond the music industry. He has become one of the world's most prominent activists, particularly in the fight against extreme poverty and HIV/AIDS in Africa. His commitment to social justice led him to co-found several influential organizations: DATA, EDUN, the ONE Campaign, and Product Red, each addressing different aspects of global inequality and development.

Bono's humanitarian work has earned him numerous prestigious honors. In 2005, Time magazine named him a Person of the Year. Queen Elizabeth II granted him an honorary knighthood in 2007, and in 2013, he was made a Commandeur of the French Ordre des Arts et des Lettres. The breadth of his influence was further recognized with his receipt of the Presidential Medal of Freedom from the United States in 2025.

Bono's maternal haplogroup V was identified through participation in the Genographic Project, as documented in a 2007 Vanity Fair article.

famous.name: Benjamin Franklin
famous.story_individual:
Benjamin Franklin was one of America's most remarkable Founding Fathers, whose diverse talents and achievements spanned politics, science, writing, and invention. Born in Boston in 1706 to a candle maker, Franklin began his career as a printer's apprentice to his brother James. After running away to Philadelphia at age 17, he established himself as a successful printer and publisher, publishing the Pennsylvania Gazette and writing Poor Richard's Almanack, which made him wealthy through its popular blend of practical wisdom and wit.

A portrait of Franklin c. 1746–1750, by Robert Feke widely believed to be the earliest known painting of Franklin.

As a scientist and inventor, Franklin conducted groundbreaking experiments with electricity, including his famous kite experiment that demonstrated lightning was a form of electricity. He invented numerous practical devices, including the lightning rod, bifocal glasses, and the Franklin stove. His scientific achievements were recognized across Europe, where he corresponded with leading intellectuals of the Enlightenment and received honorary degrees from prestigious universities including Oxford and St. Andrews. Meanwhile, his civic contributions to Philadelphia included establishing America's first lending library, founding the University of Pennsylvania, and organizing the city's first fire department.

In his later years, Franklin became one of America's most important diplomats and political leaders. He served as America's ambassador to France during the Revolutionary War, securing crucial French support for the American cause. He helped draft both the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution, and was the only person to sign all four documents fundamental to America's founding: the Declaration, the Treaty of Alliance with France, the Treaty of Paris, and the Constitution. Beyond his remarkable achievements, Franklin was known for his wit, wisdom, and dedication to self-improvement, as documented in his famous autobiography, which remains widely read today.

The first U.S postage stamp, issued in 1847 in honor of Franklin.

His mtDNA haplogroup was determined by mtFull testing of his matrilineal relative and documented on WikiTree.

Biographical information sourced from Wikipedia. Biography in part generated using Anthropic (2025) Claude 3.5 Sonnet [Large language model]. Pictures sourced from Wikimedia Commons (Public Domain).

famous.name: Sophia Palaiologina
famous.story_individual:
Grand Princess of Moscow Sophia Palaiologina, born as Zoe, emerged from a prestigious lineage that intertwined the Byzantine Empire's most elite families. Her mother, Catherine Zaccaria, represented a fascinating blend of Latin and Byzantine nobility, being the daughter of Centurione II Zaccaria, Prince of Achaea (1404-1429), and a noble Byzantine lady known as Asenina Palaiologina. Through her grandmother Asenina’s maternal line, Sophia came from the noble Tzamplakon family.

In 1472, Sophia's marriage to Ivan III of Moscow marked a pivotal moment in Russian history. She brought with her not only the legacy of the Byzantine Empire but also the sophisticated customs and culture of her heritage. Under her influence, the Moscow court underwent significant transformations, embracing more elaborate ceremonies and architectural innovations. She was instrumental in bringing Italian Renaissance architects to Moscow, contributing to the remarkable reconstruction of the Kremlin.

Sophia's legacy continued through her children, particularly her daughter Evdokia Ivanovna, who carried forward this prestigious heritage. The lineage extended further through her granddaughter Anastasia Petrovna, establishing a strong female line in the Russian royal family. All three women were buried in the Ascension Cathedral necropolis in the Moscow Kremlin, a testament to their high status in Russian society.

Recent genetic studies of remains from these burials have provided fascinating insights into this maternal lineage. The analysis revealed that Sophia, her daughter Evdokia, and her granddaughter Anastasia all shared the same maternal genetic signature, specifically the mitochondrial DNA haplogroup HV0a (which includes haplogroup V), scientifically confirming their documented relationships and preserving a direct genetic link to their Byzantine ancestors. The haplogroup was determined by testing and analyzing the hypervariable regions of the mitochondria. A more detailed haplogroup may be revealed in the future based on more detailed testing.

References

  • Kornienko, I.V., Panova, T.D., Faleeva, T.G. et al. Molecular Genetic Identification of Skeletal Remains from the Unmarked Graves of the First Half of the 16th Century from the Necropolis of the Ascension Cathedral of the Moscow Kremlin. Russ J Genet 58, 211–222 (2022). https://doi.org/10.1134/S1022795422020077

Pictured: Forensic reconstruction of Sophia Palaiologina by Sergey Nikitin, 1994, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Biography in part generated using Anthropic (2024) Claude 3.5 Sonnet [Large language model].

famous.name: Doron Behar
famous.story_individual:
Doron Behar is an Israeli physician-scientist and population geneticist. His 2012 paper introduced the Reconstructed Sapiens Reference Sequence (RSRS), which replaced reliance on the European-derived revised Cambridge Reference Sequence (rCRS) for mitochondrial DNA studies. The RSRS provided a phylogenetically meaningful reference point at the root of modern human mtDNA.

Behar served as Chief mtDNA Scientist at FamilyTreeDNA, connecting academic research with commercial genetic genealogy. His research focuses on Jewish population genetics and mitochondrial DNA studies. In 2017, he published significant findings on R1a lineages among Ashkenazi Levites, demonstrating a founder effect likely originating in Eastern Europe.

His work combines genomic analysis with historical context, producing numerous influential publications on human migration patterns and population history. His research has particularly advanced understanding of genetic heritage in Jewish and Near Eastern populations, using both mitochondrial DNA and Y-chromosome analysis to trace population origins and movements.

Pictured: Doron Behar from Who’s Who at FamilyTreeDNA (2017). Biography in part generated using Anthropic (2025) Claude 3.5 Sonnet [Large language model].

famous.name: Ruth Behar
famous.story_individual:
Ruth Behar is a renowned Cuban-American anthropologist, writer, and scholar whose work has transformed approaches to ethnographic research. Born in Havana, Cuba to a Jewish-Cuban family with diverse Sephardic Turkish and Ashkenazi Polish-Russian roots, she immigrated to the United States with her family at the age of four. After completing her undergraduate studies, Behar pursued cultural anthropology at Princeton University, where she earned her doctorate in 1983, and went on to join the Department of Anthropology at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, where she continues to serve as a professor.

Throughout her career, Behar has been a powerful advocate for acknowledging the subjective nature of anthropological research, having written and co-authored numerous books. She challenged traditional notions of detached observation by arguing that researchers should openly recognize and embrace their role as participant-observers, understanding that their own perspectives and experiences inherently shape their work. Her influential book "The Vulnerable Observer: Anthropology That Breaks Your Heart" (1996) particularly emphasized this approach.

As a multifaceted writer working across anthropology, essays, poetry, and fiction, Behar has consistently centered women's experiences and feminist perspectives in her work. Her scholarship stands out for its emotional depth and personal engagement, helping to pioneer more reflexive and humanistic approaches to anthropological research. Through her writing and teaching, she has demonstrated how scholarly work can be both rigorous and deeply personal, paving the way for more inclusive and nuanced approaches to understanding human culture and experience.

Her mtDNA haplogroup was revealed in the 2012 September-October issue of Moment Magazine.

famous.name: Agnes of Waiblingen
famous.story_individual:
Agnes of Waiblingen, also known as Agnes of Germany, Agnes of Franconia and Agnes of Saarbrücken, was a significant figure in medieval German history as the daughter of Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV and a key link between several powerful dynasties. Through her strategic marriages, she played a crucial role in shaping European politics.

First married at age 14 to Frederick I, Duke of Swabia, she had several children including Frederick II of Swabia and Conrad III, who would later become King of Germany. After Frederick's death in 1105, she married Leopold III, Margrave of Austria, with whom she had at least 11 children, including Otto of Freising, the famous medieval chronicler, and several other children who formed important political alliances through marriage.

When her brother Emperor Henry V died childless in 1125, Agnes inherited the extensive Salian family estates. This inheritance, combined with her marriages and numerous offspring, helped establish both the Hohenstaufen and Babenberg dynasties as powerful forces in medieval Germany.

An interesting fact about Agnes is that her second marriage inspired a famous legend: her lost veil, found years later by Leopold while hunting, allegedly led to his founding of the Klosterneuburg Monastery, which became an important religious and cultural center.

Her mtDNA haplogroup was reported in Christiane Maria Bauer et al, Molecular genetic investigations on Austria's patron saint Leopold III, Forensic Science International: Genetics, Volume 7, Issue 2, 2013. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fsigen.2012.10.012

Biographical information sourced in part from Wikipedia and in part from Anthropic (2025) Claude 3.5 Sonnet [Large Language Model]. Pictured: 15th century painting of Agnes by Hans Part, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

famous.name: Neanderthal Man
famous.story_individual:
Neanderthals were first named and unearthed in 1856 in the Neander Valley of Germany, three full years before Darwin published his book On the Origin of Species. In his writings, Darwin only briefly wrote about human evolution and did not mention anything about the newly named Neanderthals. Coincidentally, by 1848, a Neanderthal skeleton had already been discovered in Gibraltar. That specimen, however, had remained uncharacterized in science. So, as fate would have it, the German team is credited with discovering the new species, and the name Neanderthal still remains. Neanderthal Man (seen pictured as a reconstruction) from Feldhofer cave in Neander Valley lived approximately 40,000 years ago.

Today, we know much more about these cousins of Homo sapiens (humans), when and where they lived and how they may have mated with our stone-age ancestors. In 2008, a team led by Nobel Laureate Svante Pääbo sequenced the first Neanderthal genome, and just months after that publication, anthropologists discovered that Neanderthal DNA still resided in most humans alive today. Yes, humans and Neanderthals had mated.

Although the common evolutionary ancestor to Homo sapiens and Neanderthals lived more than half-a-million years ago, we now know that the Y chromosome of the male Neanderthals sequenced to date came from an introduction event (a mating) between a male archaic human and a female Neanderthal between 370,000 and 100,000 years ago. This, and other new findings, suggests that mixing between human ancestors and Neanderthals occurred early and possibly frequently while they co-existed for millennia in Europe and Asia, which was until approximately 35,000 years ago when Neanderthals went extinct. 

We are fortunate to be living in an amazing time where every year new discoveries add exciting information about humans, our ancestors, and our shared prehistory. The last decade alone has completely reshaped our knowledge and relationship with the once mighty Neanderthals.

Homo neanderthalensis reconstruction - Mr. N

©Neanderthal Museum

The divergence time between modern human and Neanderthal Y chromosomes was estimated by Petr et al. 2020. The evolutionary history of Neanderthal and Denisovan Y chromosomes. The A000-T haplogroup name comes from the ISOGG Y-DNA Haplogroup Tree 2019-2020.
